summary: A 1970 note commenting on the network protocol discussed in RFC 36. It is one of several responses from sites in the group on the proposals for the host-to-host protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: One person sent in comments on someone else's proposal, like friends giving feedback on a game's rules.

subtitle: Comments on the proposed ARPANET host-to-host protocol protocol multiplexing problem.

tldr.problem: RFC 36 proposed a host-to-host protocol that did not allow multiple connections to share the same network link, which could waste network resources.
tldr.mechanism: Stephen Wolfe from UCLA CCN points out two scenarios where link multiplexing would be valuable: when a single user has multiple high-speed file transfers, and when networks want to interconnect over limited links. He proposes that the protocol include socket numbers in control messages and message headers so that multiple connections can share a link.
tldr.outcome: This feedback influenced the evolution of early ARPANET protocols. It is now purely historical.

today: RFC 38 is a historical comment from the early days of ARPANET protocol design. The issues it raises were addressed in subsequent protocol designs.

sections.title: The Multiplexing Problem
sections.content: RFC 38 is a brief technical comment on RFC 36's proposed protocol. The core observation is that the protocol restricts each connection to one link, preventing multiple connections from sharing the same communication link. Wolfe argues this creates a resource bottleneck: a user with several high-speed transfers could monopolize many links, and when two independent networks connect via the ARPANET, a shortage of links could occur.
sections.plainLanguage: If every message needs its own private road to travel on, you run out of roads fast. Better to let many messages share the same road.

sections.title: Proposed Solutions
sections.content: Wolfe proposes three changes to enable multiplexing. First, the END and RDY (ready) control messages should specify socket numbers in addition to the link number, allowing the receiver to identify which connection a message belongs to. Second, the protocol should clarify whether flow control (RSM, SPD commands) applies to the whole link or to a single connection. Third, the destination socket should appear in the header of each data message on the link, in a field immediately following the header.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message should say not just which road it is on, but which car it belongs to. That way the receiving computer can sort messages from different conversations.

sections.title: Significance for Future Protocol Design
sections.content: Wolfe emphasizes that multiplexing need not be implemented immediately, but the protocol should be designed to allow it in the future. This forward-thinking approach meant reserving space for socket identifiers in control messages and data headers without requiring implementations to use multiplexing right away. The comment reflects early recognition of a fundamental networking principle: as networks grow, the ability to share resources becomes critical.
sections.plainLanguage: Wolfe is saying, 'You do not have to use multiplexing now, but leave room for it later in case we need it.' This turned out to be very wise.
